set1.q: Which mimic of deep vein thrombosis presents with leg pain, erythema, fever and chills?
opts: Lymphedema

Lymphedema is chronic edema of the extremities, usually after pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy. Chronic swelling is its hallmark, whereas leg pain with erythema, fever and chills points to cellulitis.
Cellulitis

Correct. Cellulitis causes leg pain with erythema and may be accompanied by fever and chills. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) can also bring pain, warmth and erythema, so the fever and chills are the clues that tip this mimic toward infection.
Ruptured popliteal cyst
A ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst causes severe, sudden calf discomfort that can mimic a clot. Fever, chills and erythema are not its features; that combination with leg pain describes cellulitis.
Calf muscle tear

A calf muscle pull or tear usually has an inciting injury in the history and may show bruising at the ankle. It does not explain fever and chills, which with leg pain and erythema point to cellulitis.

set1.q: Which form of immobility counts as an item in the Wells criteria?
opts: A long-haul airline flight

A long-haul flight is not among the Wells items. The immobility the score counts is being bedridden for more than 3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks, plus paralysis, paresis or a recent plaster cast of the leg.
A car trip of several hours

A car trip of several hours is not a Wells item, however long it lasts. The score counts being bedridden for more than 3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks, each patient getting 1 point for that item.
A desk job with long sitting

Long sitting at a desk is not scored in the Wells criteria. The immobility item is being bedridden for more than 3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks, and a separate item covers paralysis, paresis or recent plaster immobilization of the leg.
Bedridden for more than 3 days

Correct. The Wells item reads bedridden recently for more than 3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks, worth 1 point. Paralysis, paresis or recent plaster immobilization of the leg is a separate item; ordinary travel or sitting is not scored.

set1.q: Which examination findings characterize a healthy hemodialysis fistula?
opts: Faint thrill with no bruit

A faint thrill with no bruit is not the healthy pattern; a working fistula has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit, both with systolic and diastolic components. A missing bruit is a departure from normal.
Tender cord with overlying warmth
A tender cord with overlying warmth describes an inflamed vein, not a functioning access. A healthy fistula is marked by a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit and collapses completely with arm elevation.
Cool skin and absent pulses

Cool skin and absent pulses are not the signs of a working fistula; after access procedures, pulses are checked to make sure they have not changed from before. A healthy fistula has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit.
Diffuse thrill and soft bruit

Correct. A healthy hemodialysis arteriovenous (AV) fistula has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit, both with systolic and diastolic components, and it collapses completely when the arm is elevated. Upper arm or forearm sites are generally preferred for this access.

set1.q: Which surgery for chronic venous insufficiency is occasionally successful yet has a high rate of postoperative deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Valvuloplasty

Correct. Valvuloplasty is occasionally successful, but the incidence of postoperative deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is high. Surgery for chronic venous insufficiency aims to occlude or remove the affected vessels, restore proper flow and decrease venous hypertension.
Venous bypass

Venous bypass is described as successful in select patients, without the high postoperative clot rate. The operation that is only occasionally successful and carries a high incidence of postoperative deep vein thrombosis is valvuloplasty.
Vein stripping

Vein stripping is not the operation described with a high postoperative deep vein thrombosis rate. That description, occasionally successful with a high incidence of postoperative clot, belongs to valvuloplasty.
Injection sclerotherapy

Injection sclerotherapy is not the surgery described here. The chronic venous insufficiency operation that is only occasionally successful and has a high incidence of postoperative deep vein thrombosis is valvuloplasty.

set1.q: In the high likelihood Wells category, what does a negative D-dimer change?
opts: It calls for venography
A negative D-dimer does not route a high-likelihood patient to venography. The next step is still ultrasound of the thigh; phlebography is one option only after that ultrasound comes back negative.
It allows anticoagulation to wait

A negative D-dimer does not clear a high-likelihood patient, so it is no reason to defer decisions. Ultrasound of the thigh is still done, because the D-dimer's rule-out role applies only at low likelihood.
Nothing; ultrasound is still done

Correct. In the high-likelihood category the D-dimer is optional, and whether it is positive or negative, the patient goes to ultrasound of the thigh. The D-dimer's rule-out role applies only to low-likelihood patients.
It rules out the clot
Ruling out by D-dimer applies only to the low-likelihood category. With a high Wells score, a negative D-dimer is still followed by ultrasound of the thigh, so the result cannot close the case.

set1.q: How is a congenital arteriovenous fistula usually managed?
opts: Conservatively, with elastic support hose

Correct. Congenital arteriovenous (AV) fistulas are difficult to treat because the communications can be numerous, so they are treated conservatively with elastic support hose. Embolization can sometimes remove the fistula, whereas acquired fistulas are managed surgically.
Excision of its single communication

Congenital fistulas usually have numerous communications, not a single one, which is exactly why they are difficult to treat. They are managed conservatively with elastic support hose, with embolization sometimes able to remove the fistula.
Lifelong anticoagulation

Anticoagulation does not close an artery-to-vein connection. A congenital fistula, with its numerous communications, is managed conservatively with elastic support hose, and embolization sometimes removes it.
Thrombolysis with a filter
Thrombolysis and a vena cava filter are measures aimed at clot, and a fistula is not a clot. A congenital fistula is managed conservatively with elastic support hose, sometimes with embolization.

set1.q: Which drug class commonly causes bilateral leg swelling without signs of inflammation?
opts: Loop diuretics
Loop diuretics are not named as a cause of drug-induced edema. The classic culprit for bilateral swelling without inflammation is the dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as amlodipine.
Calcium channel blockers

Correct. Drug-induced edema is a common adverse effect of some drugs, including dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine. The swelling is often bilateral and usually shows no signs of inflammation, which separates it from deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
Low molecular weight heparins

Low molecular weight heparins are not named as a cause of drug-induced edema. Bilateral leg swelling without inflammation is a common adverse effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine.
Direct factor Xa inhibitors

Direct factor Xa inhibitors are not named as a cause of drug-induced edema. Bilateral swelling without signs of inflammation is typical of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, with amlodipine the named example.

set1.q: Without treatment, what is the cumulative rate of fatal pulmonary embolism when the embolism is symptomatic and massive?
opts: Under 1%
Under 1% is the estimate for untreated symptomatic deep vein thrombosis without pulmonary embolism, the lowest-risk group. A symptomatic massive embolism sits at the other end, at about 9%.
About 3%
About 3% is the estimate for untreated symptomatic nonmassive pulmonary embolism. The word massive moves the patient into the highest-risk group, with a cumulative fatal rate of about 9%.
About 9%

Correct. Without adequate treatment, the cumulative rate of fatal pulmonary embolism is about 9% in symptomatic massive pulmonary embolism. That compares with 3% for symptomatic nonmassive embolism and under 1% for symptomatic deep vein thrombosis (DVT) without embolism.
About 30%
About 30% overstates the highest estimate. Untreated symptomatic massive pulmonary embolism carries a cumulative fatal rate of about 9%, against 3% for nonmassive embolism.

set1.q: Prior deep vein thrombosis is one of the most common causes of which chronic condition?
opts: Superficial thrombophlebitis

Superficial thrombophlebitis is not the chronic condition that follows a deep clot. Prior deep vein thrombosis leads to chronic venous insufficiency through obstruction and scarred, incompetent valves.
Arteriovenous fistula

An arteriovenous fistula is listed as one of the other causes of chronic venous insufficiency, not a result of prior clot. Prior deep vein thrombosis is one of the most common causes of chronic venous insufficiency itself.
Peripheral artery disease

Peripheral artery disease is an arterial problem and is not what a prior venous clot causes. Prior deep vein thrombosis leads to chronic venous insufficiency, with thickened, scarred valves and proximal venous obstruction.
Chronic venous insufficiency

Correct. Prior deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is one of the most common causes of chronic venous insufficiency, even though about 25% of patients have no known history of DVT. Secondary chronic venous insufficiency comes from obstruction or valvular incompetence after a DVT, with the valve leaflets thickened and scarred.

set1.q: What is the gold standard test to confirm superficial thrombophlebitis?
opts: Computed tomography angiography

Computed tomography angiography is not the confirmatory test for superficial thrombophlebitis. The gold standard is venous duplex ultrasound, which shows a noncompressible superficial vein containing clot.
Venous duplex ultrasound

Correct. Superficial thrombophlebitis is diagnosed from history and physical examination and confirmed by venous duplex ultrasound, the gold standard. It shows a noncompressible superficial vein with clot and a thickened wall; thickening without clot would be phlebitis.
D-dimer measurement

A D-dimer is a blood test and cannot show a clot in a superficial vein. Confirmation comes from venous duplex ultrasound, the gold standard, which shows a noncompressible vein with clot and wall thickening.
Contrast ascending venography

Contrast ascending venography is not the gold standard for superficial thrombophlebitis. Venous duplex ultrasound holds that role, showing a noncompressible superficial vein with clot and a thickened wall.

set1.q: Which are the most commonly affected proximal veins in lower extremity deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Saphenous and perforator

Saphenous and perforator veins are not the deep proximal veins of the leg. The proximal veins most commonly involved in lower extremity deep vein thrombosis are the femoral and popliteal veins in the thigh.
Femoral and popliteal

Correct. In lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT), the most commonly affected proximal veins are the femoral and popliteal veins in the thigh. The most common distal veins are the peroneal veins in the calves, and in pregnancy the pelvic veins are involved.
Peroneal and tibial
The peroneal veins are the most common distal site, in the calves, not a proximal one. The most commonly affected proximal veins are the femoral and popliteal veins in the thigh.
Iliac and caval

Lower extremity clots usually begin in the calf and move proximally toward the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins, so iliac involvement reflects extension. The most commonly affected proximal veins are the femoral and popliteal veins.

set1.q: Which finding is most sensitive for a lower extremity deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Leg warmth
Warmth is 72% sensitive, the lowest of the three quoted findings for lower extremity deep vein thrombosis. Swelling, at 97%, is the most sensitive, with pain in between at 86%.
A positive Homan sign
The Homan sign is neither sensitive nor specific, so it is the weakest choice here. Leg swelling, at 97% sensitive, is the most sensitive finding for lower extremity deep vein thrombosis.
Leg swelling

Correct. Leg swelling is 97% sensitive for lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT), ahead of pain (86%) and warmth (72%). Erythema and a persisting calf cramp can also occur, while a positive Homan sign is neither sensitive nor specific.
Leg pain
Leg pain is 86% sensitive, common but behind swelling at 97%. Swelling is the most sensitive finding for lower extremity deep vein thrombosis, and warmth trails both at 72%.

set1.q: What is the mainstay of treatment for deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Anticoagulation

Correct. Anticoagulation is the mainstay of treatment for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Depending on the situation, patients may also need thrombolysis or lifelong anticoagulation, and three strategies deliver it: heparin bridged to warfarin, parenteral therapy then dabigatran or edoxaban, or oral rivaroxaban or apixaban.
Thrombolysis
Thrombolysis is something some patients may need in addition, depending on the situation, but it is not the mainstay. Anticoagulation is the mainstay of treatment for deep vein thrombosis.
Inferior vena cava filter

An inferior vena cava filter is not the mainstay of treatment. Anticoagulation is, using options such as low molecular weight heparin, unfractionated heparin, fondaparinux, the direct factor Xa inhibitors or dabigatran.
Thrombectomy
Thrombectomy is not the mainstay of deep vein thrombosis treatment. Anticoagulation is, and only some patients go on to need additional measures such as thrombolysis or lifelong anticoagulation.

set1.q: In the low likelihood Wells category, a patient's D-dimer is positive and the thigh ultrasound that follows shows no clot. What is the next step?
opts: End the work-up there

Correct. In the low-likelihood pathway a positive D-dimer leads to ultrasound of the thigh, and a negative ultrasound ends the work-up. Further imaging after a negative thigh ultrasound, such as a lower leg scan, phlebography or a repeat scan in 1 week, belongs to the high-likelihood pathway.
Rescan the thigh in a week

Rescanning the thigh in 1 week is an option after a negative thigh ultrasound in the high-likelihood pathway. This patient is in the low-likelihood pathway, where a negative thigh ultrasound ends the work-up.
Contrast venography
Phlebography (contrast venography) is an option after a negative thigh ultrasound only in the high-likelihood pathway. In the low-likelihood pathway a negative ultrasound ends the work-up.
Start anticoagulation
Anticoagulation would treat a clot that the ultrasound has just failed to show. In the low-likelihood pathway, a negative thigh ultrasound after a positive D-dimer ends the work-up.

set1.q: Erythema extending well beyond the margin of an inflamed vein raises suspicion of which condition?
opts: Lipodermatosclerosis

Lipodermatosclerosis is not among the findings of an inflamed superficial vein. Those findings are tenderness, induration and erythema along the vein, and erythema extending well beyond its margin points to septic thrombophlebitis.
Septic thrombophlebitis

Correct. Erythema that extends significantly beyond the margin of the vein should raise suspicion of septic thrombophlebitis, an infection within the vein. High fever, fluctuance and purulent drainage point the same way, and septic thrombophlebitis is uncommon without a history of venous cannulation.
Superficial phlebitis

Superficial phlebitis brings tenderness, pain, induration and erythema along the course of the vein. Redness spreading well beyond the vein's margin goes past that pattern and suggests septic thrombophlebitis, an infection within the vein.
Stasis dermatitis

Stasis dermatitis is not a sign of an inflamed superficial vein, whose findings are a tender, indurated palpable cord with erythema and warmth of the overlying skin. When that erythema extends significantly beyond the vein's margin, septic thrombophlebitis should be suspected.

set1.q: Which oral agent may help accelerate healing of venous ulcers?
opts: Furosemide

Furosemide is not the oral agent named for ulcer healing. Venous ulcers will not heal unless edema is controlled and compression is applied, and the oral drug that may help accelerate healing is aspirin.
Warfarin

Warfarin is an anticoagulant used to treat deep vein thrombosis, for example overlapped with heparin until the international normalized ratio is above 2. It is not an ulcer-healing agent; aspirin may help accelerate healing of venous ulcers.
Aspirin

Correct. Aspirin may help to accelerate healing of venous ulcers, even though no oral medication has yet been proven useful for the treatment of venous disease. Flavonoids, used to increase venous tone, are the other oral agent mentioned.
Prednisone

Corticosteroids appear in venous disease as mid-potency topical creams for stasis dermatitis, such as triamcinolone, not as oral ulcer healers. The oral agent that may help accelerate ulcer healing is aspirin.

set1.q: How long is anticoagulation given after a venous thromboembolism provoked by a minor transient risk factor?
opts: 9 to 12 months
Nine to 12 months exceeds the range for a minor transient risk factor, which is 3 to 6 months. Courses longer than that are reserved for unprovoked clots, which are treated indefinitely.
An indefinite period

An indefinite course is for an unprovoked first venous thromboembolism with no identifiable risk factor. A clot provoked by a minor transient factor has a known trigger and is treated for 3 to 6 months.
3 to 6 months

Correct. A venous thromboembolism provoked by a minor transient risk factor, such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery, prolonged travel or minor leg injury, is treated for 3 to 6 months. A major transient factor gets 3 months and an unprovoked clot is treated indefinitely.
Less than 3 months
Less than 3 months falls below the minimum initial duration of 3 months for any acute first venous thromboembolism. A minor transient risk factor is treated for 3 to 6 months.

set1.q: Why can a positive D-dimer not confirm deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Many conditions raise it

Correct. An elevated D-dimer implies increased fibrinolysis, and the test is sensitive but not specific, so conditions other than deep vein thrombosis (DVT) can raise it. A positive result therefore leads to venous duplex ultrasound to confirm a clot.
It is often falsely negative

This reverses the test's strength: D-dimer is sensitive, so false negatives are not the problem, and a negative result is useful for ruling out deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Its weakness is poor specificity, which is why a positive result cannot confirm a clot.
It detects only arterial clots

D-dimer is not limited to arterial clots; it is used as a rule-out test for deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, both venous problems. It cannot confirm a clot because it is not specific, so many conditions raise it.
It shows the clot location

D-dimer is a blood test of fibrinolysis and gives no information about where a clot is. Locating and confirming a clot takes venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity, which has replaced contrast venography.

set1.q: Older adults with a lower extremity wound need which measurement alongside the arterial pulse examination?
opts: Skin punch biopsy

A punch biopsy can help rule out other causes of an ulcer when the diagnosis is uncertain, but it is not the routine measurement paired with the pulse examination. That pairing is the ankle-brachial index.
Contrast venography

Catheter-based venography is the invasive gold standard for venous anatomy, rarely needed for diagnosis and done before an invasive intervention. The measurement paired with the arterial pulse examination is the ankle-brachial index.
Ankle-brachial index

Correct. Arterial pulse examination combined with the ankle-brachial index (ABI) should be performed on any patient with a lower extremity wound, and in older patients. History and examination alone cannot reliably exclude other causes of a leg ulcer, so the arterial side is checked directly.
D-dimer level
A D-dimer is not part of the evaluation of a leg wound. The arterial pulse examination is paired with the ankle-brachial index for any patient with a lower extremity wound and for older patients.

Correct. Post-thrombotic (postphlebitic) syndrome is symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency that follows a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), appearing from 6 to 24 months afterward. It sits on the differential of a new DVT because it also causes a swollen, symptomatic leg.
Lymphedema

Lymphedema is chronic edema of the extremities, usually with a history of pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy, not a prior clot. The complication that follows deep vein thrombosis by 6 to 24 months is post-thrombotic syndrome.
Arteriovenous fistula
An arteriovenous fistula is not the delayed sequel of a deep vein thrombosis. Symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency appearing 6 to 24 months after a clot is post-thrombotic syndrome.
Superficial thrombophlebitis

Superficial thrombophlebitis is a separate condition on the differential of deep vein thrombosis, not its delayed consequence. The complication that follows a clot by 6 to 24 months is post-thrombotic syndrome, symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency.

Weeks to months

Several days

set1.q: What underlies the wide spectrum of abnormalities in chronic venous disease?
opts: Chronic arterial hypoperfusion

Chronic arterial hypoperfusion is not among the causes of chronic venous disease. Its spectrum is driven by elevated venous pressure, from inadequate muscle pump function, incompetent valves with reflux, venous thrombosis or other venous obstruction.
Lymphatic vessel obstruction

Lymphatic vessel obstruction is not what drives chronic venous disease. The underlying problem is venous hypertension, from a failing muscle pump, incompetent valves with reflux, thrombosis or other venous obstruction.
Loss of plasma protein into tissue

Loss of plasma protein into tissue is not the mechanism. Chronic venous disease is a pressure problem in the veins: diseased valves let blood move in both directions, elevating venous pressure, which leads to dilation, skin changes and ulceration.
Venous hypertension

Correct. Venous hypertension, elevated venous pressure, underlies many of the wide spectrum of abnormalities of chronic venous disease, from telangiectasias to varicose veins to chronic venous insufficiency. It triggers a sequence of venous dilation, then skin changes and ulceration.

set1.q: What is first-line management of uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis?
opts: Inferior vena cava filter

An inferior vena cava filter is not part of treating superficial thrombophlebitis, which rarely causes serious complications and rarely embolizes. First-line care is warm compresses, compression, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug.
Anticoagulation for three months

Anticoagulation is added only when clot burden is extensive or thrombotic risk is intermediate or higher, and this case is uncomplicated. First-line management is warm compresses, compression, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug such as ibuprofen.
Warm compresses and ibuprofen

Correct. Uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis rarely causes serious complications, and typical treatment is warm compresses, compression, elevation of the limb and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) such as ibuprofen or diclofenac. Thrombolysis with alteplase

Thrombolysis is not used for uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis, which rarely embolizes. Warm compresses, compression, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug are first-line, with a repeat examination within 7 to 10 days.

set1.q: Intermittent pneumatic compression prevents clots chiefly by countering which component of the Virchow triad?
opts: Venous stasis

Correct. Intermittent pneumatic compression squeezes the leg in sequence from the lower leg upward, pushing blood along and countering venous stasis. It is used especially when a patient must be immobilized after surgery or during a long hospital stay.
Hypercoagulable state

A compression sleeve acts on the leg from outside and does not change the blood's tendency to clot. Its sequential squeezing moves blood out of a still leg, which addresses stasis in patients immobilized after surgery or in a long hospital stay.
Endothelial trauma

External compression does not repair or protect the vessel lining, so it does not address endothelial trauma. The device works by moving blood out of an immobilized leg in sequential waves, which counters stasis.
All three components

The device works through one mechanism, sequential squeezing that moves blood out of an immobilized leg. That counters venous stasis only, leaving the hypercoagulable state and endothelial trauma untouched.

set1.q: Andexanet alfa is the reversal agent for which pair of anticoagulants?

Dabigatran is reversed by idarucizumab, not andexanet alfa, and fondaparinux is not among the drugs andexanet alfa reverses. Its pair is apixaban and rivaroxaban, with off-label use for edoxaban.
Apixaban and rivaroxaban

Correct. Andexanet alfa (Andexxa) is the reversal agent for apixaban and rivaroxaban when either causes life-threatening or intracranial hemorrhage, the most serious adverse effect of anticoagulation. It is also used off-label for edoxaban.
Dabigatran and warfarin

Each of these has its own reversal agent: dabigatran is reversed by idarucizumab, and warfarin by 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, fresh frozen plasma or vitamin K. Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.
Heparin and enoxaparin

set1.q: Prolonged bedridden inactivity raises superficial thrombophlebitis risk. Which Virchow triad component does immobilization represent?
opts: Arterial insufficiency

Arterial insufficiency is not a component of the Virchow triad, which is venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and vascular endothelial injury. Bedridden inactivity is immobilization, listed under venous stasis.
Venous stasis

Correct. Immobilization, such as long flights, prolonged sitting or postoperative inactivity, is listed under venous stasis, the altered blood flow component of the Virchow triad. Being bedridden alters blood flow in the leg veins rather than injuring them or changing the blood's clotting tendency.
Hypercoagulable state

A hypercoagulable state is the clotting-tendency component, from inherited causes such as factor V Leiden or acquired ones such as cancer, estrogen or pregnancy. Immobility alters blood flow instead, which is venous stasis.
Endothelial trauma

Endothelial injury comes from trauma, surgery, intravenous drug use and burns, which damage the vessel lining. Lying in bed does not injure the vein; it alters blood flow, which places it under venous stasis.

opts: Stasis, hypertension, endothelial trauma

Hypertension appears among the deep vein thrombosis risk factors, but it is not one of the three components; only stasis and endothelial trauma are right here. The triad is venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and endothelial trauma.
Stasis, infection, vessel spasm

Infection and vessel spasm are not triad components, so only stasis is right in this set. The Virchow triad is venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state (inherited or acquired) and vascular endothelial injury.
Immobility, anemia, dehydration

Immobility is a cause of the stasis component, not a component in its own right, and anemia and dehydration are not part of the triad. The triad is venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and endothelial trauma.
Stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial trauma

opts: Plasma D-dimer

Magnetic resonance venography

Contrast ascending venography

Correct. Contrast ascending venography is the definitive gold standard for diagnosing deep vein thrombosis (DVT). In practice it has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity, which is why the gold standard and the usual first imaging test differ.

Family history

The lateral malleolus, the outer ankle, is not where venous itching usually begins. Pruritus of chronic venous disease often starts around the medial malleolus, on the inner side of the ankle, so a medial start is the venous pattern.
Over the dorsum of the foot

The dorsum of the foot is not the usual starting site. Itching in chronic venous disease often starts around the medial malleolus, along with leg heaviness or swelling that is worse with prolonged standing.
Behind the knee in the popliteal fossa

Around the medial malleolus

The Homan sign is neither sensitive nor specific, so it has neither property. Swelling, at 97% sensitivity, is the presenting finding that best catches deep vein thrombosis.
Neither sensitive nor specific

Correct. A patient with deep vein thrombosis (DVT) may have a positive Homan sign, but it is neither sensitive nor specific. Swelling (97% sensitive), pain (86%) and warmth (72%) are the more useful presenting findings.
Sensitive but not specific

Sensitive but not specific describes a finding that rarely misses disease, which the Homan sign does not achieve. Of the presenting findings, swelling is the sensitive one at 97%; the Homan sign is neither sensitive nor specific.

opts: One point
One point is the value of each positive item, such as active cancer or calf swelling over 3 cm. The alternative diagnosis item works in the other direction and subtracts 2 points.
Two points

Correct. An alternative diagnosis at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) scores minus 2, the only negative item in the Wells criteria. Every other item adds 1 point, and the total sorts patients into low (zero or less), moderate (1 to 2) or high (3 or more) likelihood.
Three points

set2.q: After parenteral therapy for 5 days, which agents can anticoagulation be switched to?
opts: Rivaroxaban or apixaban

Rivaroxaban and apixaban are the oral monotherapy strategy, given as a loading dose followed by a maintenance dose with no parenteral lead-in. The anticoagulants that follow 5 days of parenteral therapy are dabigatran and edoxaban.
Warfarin or heparin

Warfarin and heparin form the classical but waning strategy, which starts with heparin and bridges to warfarin rather than switching after 5 days of parenteral therapy. The agents taken up after a 5-day parenteral lead-in are dabigatran and edoxaban.
Aspirin or clopidogrel

Dabigatran or edoxaban

Correct. set2.q: What is the primary presenting symptom of chronic venous insufficiency?
opts: Cool, pale toes

Cool, pale toes are not part of chronic venous insufficiency, which presents first with progressive pitting edema of the lower leg. Later changes are dermatitis, shiny taut ankle skin and brownish hemosiderin pigmentation.
Numbness across the foot

Progressive pitting edema

Correct. Progressive pitting edema of the leg, usually the lower leg, is the primary presenting symptom of chronic venous insufficiency. It usually comes with dull discomfort worsened by standing, and pruritic dermatitis and brownish pigmentation follow over time.
Calf pain when walking

set2.q: Which history typically accompanies lymphedema when it mimics deep vein thrombosis?
opts: A recent long flight

A recent long flight is not the history linked to lymphedema. Lymphedema is chronic edema of the extremities, usually accompanied by pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy, so the tell is a long-standing swelling with a pelvic or cancer history, not a recent trip.
Starting a new blood pressure drug

Starting a new drug fits drug-induced edema, a common adverse effect of some drugs such as dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine), with swelling that is often bilateral and lacks inflammation. Lymphedema instead follows pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy.

A sudden injury fits a calf muscle pull or tear, where the inciting injury is usually part of the history and bruising may appear at the ankle. Lymphedema is chronic edema linked to pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy, not to an acute event.
Pelvic surgery or radiation

About 3%

About 9%

About 25%

set2.q: What defines superficial phlebitis?
opts: Vein wall inflammation without a clot

Correct. Superficial phlebitis is inflammation of the wall of a vein in the absence of thrombus. When a clot is present in the inflamed vein, the condition is called superficial thrombophlebitis, so the presence or absence of clot is the dividing line.
Vein wall inflammation with a clot

Vein wall inflammation with a clot is superficial thrombophlebitis, defined as phlebitis with thrombus. Superficial phlebitis is the same inflammation without a clot, so this choice describes the other condition.
Infected vein wall with pus
Pus and infection are not part of the definition of superficial phlebitis. Phlebitis is inflammation of the wall of a vein without thrombus; add a clot and it becomes superficial thrombophlebitis.
Clot within a deep leg vein

A clot in a deep leg vein is deep vein thrombosis, a different disorder from phlebitis. Superficial phlebitis is inflammation of the wall of a superficial vein with no thrombus at all, and adding a clot makes it superficial thrombophlebitis.

set2.q: In the Wells criteria, calf swelling counts when it exceeds what difference from the other leg?
opts: More than 1 cm

More than 1 cm is below the threshold, so a 2 cm difference would not score. The Wells item requires calf swelling more than 3 cm larger than the other leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity.
More than 3 cm

Correct. Calf swelling scores 1 point when the calf is more than 3 cm larger than the other leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. Measuring at that fixed point keeps the comparison between the two legs consistent.
More than 5 cm

More than 5 cm sets the bar too high and would miss calves 4 cm larger, which already score. The item counts calf swelling more than 3 cm larger than the other leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity.
More than 10 cm
Ten centimeters is the measuring point below the tibial tuberosity, not the size threshold. The calf must be more than 3 cm larger than the other leg at that point for the item to score.

set2.q: Under the Virchow triad, cancer belongs to which component?
opts: Venous stasis
Venous stasis covers altered blood flow from immobilization, venous insufficiency and heart failure. Cancer is not a flow problem; it is listed as an acquired hypercoagulable state.
Endothelial trauma

Endothelial injury covers trauma, surgery, intravenous drug use and burns, all of which damage the vessel lining. Cancer is listed instead under the hypercoagulable state, as an acquired clotting tendency.
None of the three

Cancer does appear in the Virchow triad, so this choice is wrong. It sits in the hypercoagulable state, with oral contraceptives, estrogen replacement and pregnancy, and is also listed separately as a deep vein thrombosis risk factor.
Hypercoagulable state

Correct. Cancer is listed under the hypercoagulable state of the Virchow triad, an acquired clotting tendency alongside oral contraceptives, postmenopausal estrogen replacement and pregnancy. Inherited examples in the same component include factor V Leiden and protein C or S deficiency.

set2.q: Which component of the Virchow triad includes postoperative inactivity?
opts: Venous stasis

Correct. Immobilization, including long flights, prolonged sitting and postoperative inactivity, is listed under venous stasis, the altered blood flow component of the Virchow triad. Immobilization carries about a 20-fold increased risk for deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
Hypercoagulable state

A hypercoagulable state is a clotting tendency of the blood, inherited (factor V Leiden) or acquired (cancer, estrogen, pregnancy). Postoperative inactivity changes blood flow, not clotting tendency, so it belongs to venous stasis.
Endothelial trauma

Endothelial injury covers the operation itself, especially knee or hip replacement or hip fracture surgery, along with trauma and burns. The inactivity that follows is a separate factor, immobilization, which is venous stasis.
Turbulent arterial flow

Turbulent arterial flow is not one of the three Virchow components, which are venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and endothelial injury. Postoperative inactivity is immobilization, listed under venous stasis.

set2.q: For which clot may thrombolysis be considered in deep vein thrombosis?
opts: A large proximal clot

Correct. Thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is helpful for a large proximal deep vein thrombosis (DVT), or for a pulmonary embolism in a hemodynamically stable patient. Thrombectomy is the other option for removing clot directly.
An isolated calf clot

An isolated calf clot is not the setting for thrombolysis. Tissue plasminogen activator is described as helpful for a large proximal deep vein thrombosis or a stable pulmonary embolism, not a small distal clot.
A superficial vein clot

A superficial vein clot is not a deep vein thrombosis and is not treated with thrombolysis. Tissue plasminogen activator is considered for a large proximal deep vein thrombosis or a pulmonary embolism in a stable patient.
Any clot with active bleeding

Active bleeding is the setting where an inferior vena cava filter is used for an acute proximal leg clot, because anticoagulation is contraindicated. Thrombolysis is considered for a large proximal clot, not for a bleeding patient.

set2.q: For how long after delivery does postpartum status raise deep vein thrombosis risk?
opts: The first 6 to 12 weeks

Correct. The first 6 to 12 weeks postpartum is listed among the risk factors for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Pregnancy itself is a hypercoagulable state in the Virchow triad, and the raised risk carries through those weeks after delivery.
The first 2 weeks only
Two weeks is too short a window. The listed period of raised deep vein thrombosis risk runs through the first 6 to 12 weeks after delivery, so a woman at week 5 postpartum is still at risk.
The first 6 months
Six months overshoots the listed window. Postpartum deep vein thrombosis risk is listed for the first 6 to 12 weeks after delivery, about 3 months at most, not half a year.
The first 2 years
Two years is far beyond the listed window. Postpartum status raises deep vein thrombosis risk for the first 6 to 12 weeks after delivery, so the risk is measured in weeks, not years.

set2.q: What is the purpose of emollients in venous skin care?
opts: Shrink the dilated veins
Emollients work on the skin, not the veins. Compressing dilated veins is the job of compression therapy with hosiery or bandages, which also decreases edema and reduces inflammation.
Dissolve deeper skin scarring

Emollients do not dissolve scarring; their role is to maintain the skin barrier, preventing dryness and fissuring and reducing scratching. Compression therapy is the measure that acts below the skin, improving oxygen transport to the skin and subcutaneous tissues.
Prevent new clot formation

Emollients have no role in clot prevention; they maintain the skin barrier, preventing dryness, fissuring and scratching. Management of chronic venous insufficiency targets edema and skin health through elevation, exercise and compression.
Maintain the skin barrier

Correct. Emollients such as Vaseline or Lubriderm maintain the skin barrier, preventing dryness and fissuring and reducing scratching. Skin care is part of initial nonoperative management of chronic venous insufficiency, along with leg elevation, exercise and compression.

opts: By skin punch biopsy

A skin punch biopsy samples tissue and cannot show an abnormal artery-to-vein connection. The diagnosis of a fistula is made by physical examination, with computed tomography angiography or angiography to confirm location and size.
By ankle-brachial index

The ankle-brachial index is not the basis of the diagnosis. An arteriovenous fistula is diagnosed by physical examination, and imaging such as computed tomography angiography, angiography or duplex ultrasound confirms it.
By physical examination

Correct. The diagnosis of an arteriovenous (AV) fistula is determined by physical examination. Computed tomography angiography and angiography can then confirm it and give the location and size, and duplex ultrasound confirms suspected iatrogenic fistulas after groin access.
By D-dimer measurement

A D-dimer is a blood test and cannot show whether an artery connects to a vein. Arteriovenous fistulas are diagnosed by physical examination and then confirmed with computed tomography angiography or angiography.

set2.q: Where should a patient with a venous ulcer be referred for care?
opts: A pain management clinic
A pain management clinic does not provide what a venous ulcer needs to heal: edema control and compression. The referral for ulcer care is wound care management, where healing can take 4 to 6 months.
Wound care management

Correct. Venous ulcers are referred to wound care management, where complete healing can take 4 to 6 months. Ulcers will not heal unless edema is controlled and compression is applied, and an ulcer that does not fully heal needs further workup for infection or other causes.
A hematology clinic
A hematology clinic is not where ulcer care happens. Venous ulcers are referred to wound care management, and they heal only once edema is controlled and compression is applied.
A rheumatology clinic
A rheumatology clinic is not the referral for an ulcer of venous origin. Venous ulcers go to wound care management, and healing depends on controlling edema and applying compression.

set2.q: An elevated D-dimer implies increased activity of which process?
opts: Vitamin K depletion

Vitamin K depletion is not what a D-dimer measures. An elevated D-dimer implies increased fibrinolysis, so it rises when fibrin clot is being broken down, and that sensitivity is what makes a negative result useful for ruling out deep vein thrombosis.
Red cell destruction

Red cell destruction is not what a D-dimer reports; the test reflects fibrinolysis, the breakdown of fibrin. That is why it is used in suspected deep vein thrombosis as a sensitive marker that rules a clot out when negative but cannot confirm one when positive.
Fibrinolysis

Correct. D-dimer elevation implies increased fibrinolysis, the breakdown of fibrin clot. Because it is sensitive but not specific, it serves as a rule-out test for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism: a negative result in a low-risk patient ends the work-up, while a positive one leads to ultrasound.
Platelet production

opts: Pain relieved by warm compresses

Extensive clot or higher thrombosis risk

Correct. Anticoagulation may be started when the clot burden is extensive or the patient is at intermediate or higher risk of thrombosis, using unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin or fondaparinux. Otherwise warm compresses, compression, elevation and anti-inflammatory drugs are the typical treatment.
Any tender palpable cord in a leg

Purulent drainage over the vein

set2.q: How is the D-dimer characterized as a test for deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Both sensitive and specific

A test both sensitive and specific could confirm a clot on its own, and D-dimer cannot. It is sensitive but not specific, so a positive result leads to ultrasound while a negative one helps rule out a clot.
Neither sensitive nor specific
Neither sensitive nor specific undersells the test: D-dimer is sensitive, which is why a negative result can rule out deep vein thrombosis in a low-risk patient. Its weakness is specificity alone.
Sensitive but not specific

Correct. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific: elevation implies increased fibrinolysis, so a positive result can occur without a clot. That profile makes it a rule-out test for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism, where a negative result in a low-risk patient ends the work-up.
Specific but not sensitive

This reverses the profile. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, so it rarely misses a clot yet can be elevated without one; that is why a negative result rules out and a positive one needs ultrasound.
